name: bluewater-07-invisible-work
lines: Saturday morning. Jen needs a new fence. She does what everybody does.
She picks up her phone and looks at two fence builders. Both are ten minutes from her house.
One has forty videos of real fences. The other has two blurry photos from six years ago.
She calls the one with the videos. He is the worse builder.
The one with the blurry photos is Ray. Ray is not real. His problem is everywhere.
Eighteen years building fences. Straight lines. Posts set in concrete. They do not lean.
And this is Cole. Three years in. His gates sag by spring.
But Cole does one thing Ray never does. He takes out his phone on every job.
Before. During. After. Thirty seconds. Posted that night.
So when Jen looks them both up, Cole looks busy. Ray looks closed.
Jen does not know Ray is better. She only knows what she can see.
Say that costs Ray one job a month.
At six thousand dollars a fence, that is seventy two thousand dollars a year.
Going to a gate that sags.
Ray's work is standing in forty backyards across town. Behind forty closed gates.
That night Ray scrolls through Cole's page. Forty videos. Forty happy customers.
Then he looks at his own. Two photos. The newest one is six years old.
Eighteen years of work, and not one minute of it on camera.
Ray is not losing on the work. He is losing because nobody can see the work.
So Ray decides to show it.
First, the truth about content. People do not want a show. They want proof.
Proof that you are real. Proof that you are good. Proof that you are still in business.
You do not need a camera crew. You need the phone in your pocket and three kinds of video.
None of them take more than a minute to film.
And none of them need you to dance, point at words, or be funny.
Video one. The before and after.
Film the old fence. Ten seconds. Say what was wrong with it.
Film the new one from the same spot. Ten seconds.
That is the whole video. The work does the talking.
Do not add music. Do not add a filter. Just the fence.
Ray films his first one on a Tuesday. It takes him forty seconds.
Video two. Answer the question every customer asks.
How much does a fence cost? How long does it take? Cedar or vinyl?
Ray gets those three questions every week. Each one is a video.
Look at the camera. Say your name and your town. Then answer it the way you would at the kitchen table.
Do not read a script. If you can say it to a customer, you can say it to a phone.
Ray's first try is terrible. He posts it anyway. By the tenth, he is not thinking about it.
Here is a trick. Open your texts. Every question a customer has sent you this year is a video waiting to be filmed.
Video three. Show the part nobody sees.
The concrete around the post. The level on the rail. The cleanup at the end.
This is the video that sells, because it shows what they are paying for.
Cole cannot film that. He does not do it.
Customers cannot judge a fence. But they can see who takes care.
Now the how. Keep it simple.
Hold the phone upright. Stand with the sun behind you. Wipe the lens on your shirt.
Film across the yard, not down at your boots. Let them see the whole job.
Say your name and your town in the first three seconds.
Keep it under one minute. Add captions. Many people watch with the sound off.
And always ask the customer before you film their yard.
Then post the same video everywhere. Your Google profile. Instagram. Facebook. YouTube.
One video, four places. Ten minutes.
Start with your Google profile. That is where people look you up.
Put your phone number in every caption. And reply to every comment.
Do it every week. One video a week beats ten in one day and then silence.
Save every video in one folder on your phone. In a year you will have fifty.
What should you never post? Other people's videos. Politics. Anything you would not say at a customer's door.
Meanwhile, Cole gets lazy. He starts posting stock photos and discount ads.
No face. No real jobs. His page looks like a flyer.
People scroll right past it. An ad is not proof.
Three months later. Saturday morning. Another homeowner needs a fence.
He looks up two builders.
This time Ray has twelve videos. Real fences. His face. His town.
The first one is a leaning fence. The second is the same yard, straight as a ruler.
He watches one more. Then he calls.
No music. No tricks. Just a straight fence and the man who built it.
Ray's phone rings in the truck. Six thousand dollars. To the right builder this time.
Nobody can promise a video will bring you a job. Most will not.
But every one is proof. And proof adds up.
Ray did not become a creator. He stayed a fence builder who films.
It takes ten minutes a job. Your work is already good. Let people see it.
One extra job a month was seventy two thousand dollars for Ray. Work out yours.
So do this tonight. Look yourself up the way a stranger would.
If your newest photo is older than your truck, start this week.
One before and after. One answer. One thing nobody sees.
That is all of it. If you want a hand, we are Bluewater Co.
